props.title: Mona Lisa
props.initialSlug: Ex-con driver falls for mysterious call girl

sections.content: Mona Lisa stands as one of the great British neo-noirs, with Bob Hoskins delivering a career-defining performance as George, an ex-con turned chauffeur for a high-class prostitute. The film masterfully blends elements from classic film noir like Taxi Driver (1976) and The Long Good Friday (1980), but adds a distinctly British working-class perspective. Director Neil Jordan crafts a gritty London underworld that feels both dangerous and deeply human, while Michael Caine's chilling portrayal of crime boss Mortwell provides the perfect counterpoint to Hoskins' vulnerable tough guy.

sections.content: The film's exploration of class dynamics and moral ambiguity shares DNA with other British crime classics like The Hit (1984) and Performance (1970). But what sets Mona Lisa apart is its emotional core - the complex relationship between George and Simone (Cathy Tyson). Their dynamic echoes noir classics like The Big Sleep (1946), but with a contemporary examination of power, gender, and exploitation that feels thoroughly modern.

Jordan's direction shows remarkable restraint, allowing London's seedy underbelly to emerge organically rather than sensationalizing it. The film's visual style draws from both British kitchen sink realism and American noir, creating a unique aesthetic that influenced later UK crime films like Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels (1998) and Layer Cake (2004). sections.content: Mona Lisa emerged during a vital period for neo-noir, alongside films like Blue Velvet (1986) and Angel Heart (1987). These films updated noir conventions for the 1980s while maintaining the genre's core themes of moral corruption and doomed romance. The film's success paved the way for Jordan's later work, particularly The Crying Game (1992), which similarly deals with identity and forbidden attraction.
